Heegaard Floer correction terms and rational genus bounds

Yi NI Zhongtao WU Note: Corresponding author Note: Present address: Department of Mathematics, The Chinese Universiy of Hong Kong, Shatin, Hong Kong, Email : ztwu@math.cuhk.edu.hk Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Caltech, MC 253-37 Affiliation: 1200 E California Blvd, Pasadena, CA 91125 Email: Email: yini@caltech.edu zhongtao@caltech.edu
Abstract

Given an element in the first homology of a rational homology 33–sphere YY, one can consider the minimal rational genus of all knots in this homology class. This defines a function Θ\Theta on H1​(Y,ℤ)H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z}), which was introduced by Turaev as an analogue of Thurston norm. We will give a lower bound for this function using the correction terms in Heegaard Floer homology. As a corollary, we show that Floer simple knots in L-spaces are genus minimizers in their homology classes, hence answer questions of Turaev and Rasmussen about genus minimizers in lens spaces.

1 Introduction

Heegaard Floer homology, introduced by Ozsváth and Szabó [16], has been very successful in the study of low-dimensional topology. One important feature of Heegaard Floer homology which makes it so useful is that it gives a lower bound for the genus of surfaces in a given homology class. In dimension 33, it determines the Thurston norm [22]. In dimension 44, the adjunction inequality [18] gives a lower bound to the genus of surfaces which is often sharp, and the concordance invariant [21] gives a lower bound to the slice genus of knots. Such kind of results have been known before in Donaldson theory and Seiberg–Witten theory [5, 6, 7, 11, 8], but the combinatorial nature of Heegaard Floer homology makes the corresponding results easier to use in many problems.

In this paper, we will study a new type of genus bounds. Suppose that YY is a closed oriented 33–manifold, there is a kind of “norm” function one can define on the torsion subgroup of H1​(Y,ℤ)H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z}). To define it, let us first recall the rational genus of a rationally null-homologous knot K⊂YK\subset Y defined by Calegari and Gordon [3].

Suppose that KK is a rationally null-homologous oriented knot in YY, and ν⁡(K)\nu(K) is a tubular neighborhood of KK. A properly embedded oriented connected surface F⊂Y\ν∘​(K)F\subset Y\backslash\overset{\circ}{\nu}(K) is called a rational Seifert surface for KK, if ∂F\partial F consists of coherently oriented parallel curves on ∂ν⁡(K)\partial\nu(K), and the orientation of ∂F\partial F is coherent with the orientation of KK. The rational genus of KK is defined to be

‖K‖=minF⁡max⁡{0,−χ⁡(F)}2​|[μ]⋅[∂F]|,||K||=\min_{F}\frac{\max\{0,-\chi(F)\}}{2|[\mu]\cdot[\partial F]|},

where FF runs over all the rational Seifert surfaces for KK, and μ⊂∂ν⁡(K)\mu\subset\partial\nu(K) is the meridian of KK.

The rational genus is a natural generalization of the genus of null-homologous knots. Moreover, given a torsion class in H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y), one can consider the minimal rational genus for all knots in this torsion class. More precisely, given a∈Tors​H1​(Y)a\in\mathrm{Tors}H_{1}(Y), let

Θ⁡(a)=minK⊂Y,[K]=a⁡2​‖K‖.\Theta(a)=\min_{K\subset Y,\>[K]=a}2||K||.

This Θ\Theta was introduced by Turaev [28] in a slightly different form. Turaev regarded Θ\Theta as an analogue of Thurston norm [27], in the sense that it measures the minimal normalized Euler characteristic of a “folded surface” representing a given class in H2​(Y,ℚ/ℤ)H_{2}(Y;\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}).

In [28], Turaev gave a lower bound for Θ\Theta in terms of his torsion function. When b1​(Y)>0b_{1}(Y)>0, Turaev’s torsion function is a kind of Euler characteristic of Heegaard Floer homology [17], so his lower bound can be reformulated in terms of Heegaard Floer homology. (One can even expect to get a better bound with Heegaard Floer homology.) When b1​(Y)=0b_{1}(Y)=0, the relationship between Turaev’s torsion function and Heegaard Floer homology is not very clear in the literature. Nevertheless, our following theorem gives an independent lower bound in terms of the correction terms d⁡(Y,𝔰)d(Y,\mathfrak{s}) in Heegaard Floer homology [19].

Theorem 1.1.

Suppose that YY is a rational homology 33–sphere, K⊂YK\subset Y is a knot, FF is a rational Seifert surface for KK. Then

1+−χ⁡(F)|[∂F]⋅[μ]|≥max𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)⁡{d⁡(Y,𝔰+PD⁡[K])−d⁡(Y,𝔰)}.1+\frac{-\chi(F)}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}\geq\max_{\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y)}\big\{d(Y,\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K])-d(Y,\mathfrak{s})\big\}. (1)

The right hand side of (1) only depends on the manifold YY and the homology class of KK, so it gives a lower bound for 1+Θ⁡(a)1+\Theta(a) for the homology class a=[K]a=[K].

We find Theorem 1.1 quite interesting because it unveils some topological information contained in Heegaard Floer homology of rational homology spheres. Such information is relatively rare in the literature comparing to the case of manifolds with positive b1b_{1}, where one can get useful information like Thurston norm [22] and fibration [13].

Theorem 1.1 is particularly useful when YY is an L-space and the homology class contains a Floer simple knot. Recall that a rational homology 33–sphere YY is an L-space if rank​H​F^​(Y)=|H1​(Y,ℤ)|\mathrm{rank}\widehat{HF}(Y)=|H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z})|. A rationally null-homologous knot KK in a 33–manifold YY is Floer simple if rank​H​F​K^​(Y,K)=rank​H​F^​(Y)\mathrm{rank}\widehat{HFK}(Y,K)=\mathrm{rank}\widehat{HF}(Y).

Theorem 1.2.

Suppose that YY is an L-space, KK is a Floer simple knot in YY. If K1K_{1} is another knot in YY with [K1]=[K]∈H1​(Y,ℤ)[K_{1}]=[K]\in H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z}), then

‖K‖≤‖K1‖.||K||\leq||K_{1}||.

An important class of L-spaces is lens spaces. The question of computing Θ\Theta for lens spaces was first considered by Turaev [28]. The lower bound given by Turaev (for any manifold) is always less than 11, but the value of Θ\Theta can be much larger than 11 even for lens spaces. For example, if a∼p2a\sim\frac{p}{2}, using (16) in Section 5 we get a lower bound ∼p4\sim\frac{p}{4} for Θ⁡(a)\Theta(a) in L⁡(p,1)L(p,1). So Turaev’s bound is not sharp for lens spaces.

Hedden [4] and Rasmussen [26] observed that for any 11–dimensional homology class in a lens space, there exists a knot in this homology class which is Floer simple. Let U0∪U1U_{0}\cup U_{1} be a genus 11 Heegaard splitting of a lens space L⁡(p,q)L(p,q), and let D0,D1D_{0},D_{1} be meridian disks in U0,U1U_{0},U_{1} such that ∂D0∩∂D1\partial D_{0}\cap\partial D_{1} consists of exactly pp points. A knot in L⁡(p,q)L(p,q) is called simple if it is either the unknot or the union of two arcs a0⊂D0a_{0}\subset D_{0} and a1⊂D1a_{1}\subset D_{1}. Up to isotopy there is exactly one simple knot in each homology class in H1​(L​(p,q))H_{1}(L(p,q)), and every simple knot is Floer simple.

Rasmussen [26] conjectured that simple knots are genus minimizers in their homology classes, and verified this conjecture for dual Berge knots. In fact, he proved that primitive knots in L-spaces with rational genus less than 12\frac{1}{2} are genus minimizing. As a consequence of our Theorem 1.2, we verify Rasmussen’s conjecture in general.

Corollary 1.3.

Simple knots in lens spaces are genus minimizers in their homology classes.

Remark 1.4.

Rasmussen also conjectured that simple knots are the unique genus minimizers in their homology classes. As pointed out in [4, 26], the uniqueness of genus minimizers in lens spaces would imply the Berge Conjecture on lens space surgeries [2].

Unlike the Heegaard Floer bound for Thurston norm, our bound for Θ\Theta is not always sharp. For example, suppose K⊂YK\subset Y is a knot in a homology sphere such that the half degree of its Alexander polynomial is equal to its genus gg. Let p≥4​g−2p\geq 4g-2 be an integer, Yp​(K)Y_{p}(K) be the manifold obtained by pp–surgery on KK, and K′⊂Yp​(K)K^{\prime}\subset Y_{p}(K) be the dual knot of the surgery. Then the lower bound given by Turaev on Θ⁡([K′])\Theta([K^{\prime}]) in Yp​(K)Y_{p}(K) is 2​g−1p\frac{2g-1}{p}, and can be obviously realized [28, Section 6.2]. In this case, the bound given by Theorem 1.1 is not always sharp (see Section 5). Nevertheless, using Heegaard Floer homology we will prove the following result.

Proposition 1.5.

Suppose that K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot with genus gg, and that p≥2​gp\geq 2g is an integer, then the dual knot K′⊂Sp3​(K)K^{\prime}\subset S^{3}_{p}(K) is a genus minimizer in its homology class. Namely, Θ⁡([K′])=2​g−1p\Theta([K^{\prime}])=\frac{2g-1}{p}.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we will give the necessary background on Heegaard Floer homology. We will focus on the construction of the knot Floer homology of rationally null-homologous knots. In Section 3, we prove a symmetry relation in knot Floer homology. In Section 4, we prove Theorem 1.1 by analyzing the knot Floer chain complex of rationally null-homologous knots. In Section 5, we apply Theorem 1.1 to some examples, thus prove Theorem 1.2 and Proposition 1.5.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Correction terms in Heegaard Floer homology

Heegaard Floer homology, introduced by Ozsváth and Szabó [16], is an invariant for closed oriented Spinc 33–manifolds (Y,𝔰)(Y,\mathfrak{s}), taking the form of a collection of related homology groups as H​F^​(Y,𝔰)\widehat{HF}(Y,\mathfrak{s}), H​F±​(Y,𝔰)HF^{\pm}(Y,\mathfrak{s}), and H​F∞​(Y,𝔰)HF^{\infty}(Y,\mathfrak{s}). There is a UU–action on Heegaard Floer homology groups. When 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is torsion, there is an absolute Maslov ℚ\mathbb{Q}–grading on the Heegaard Floer homology groups. The UU–action decreases the grading by 22.

For a rational homology 33–sphere YY with a Spinc structure 𝔰\mathfrak{s}, H​F+​(Y,𝔰)HF^{+}(Y,\mathfrak{s}) can be decomposed as the direct sum of two groups: the first group is the image of H​F∞​(Y,𝔰)≅ℤ⁡[U,U−1]HF^{\infty}(Y,\mathfrak{s})\cong\mathbb{Z}[U,U^{-1}] in H​F+​(Y,𝔰)HF^{+}(Y,\mathfrak{s}), which is isomorphic to 𝒯+=ℤ⁡[U,U−1]/U​Z​[U]\mathcal{T}^{+}=\mathbb{Z}[U,U^{-1}]/UZ[U], and its minimal absolute ℚ\mathbb{Q}–grading is an invariant of (Y,𝔰)(Y,\mathfrak{s}), denoted by d⁡(Y,𝔰)d(Y,\mathfrak{s}), the correction term [19]; the second group is the quotient modulo the above image and is denoted by H​Fred​(Y,𝔰)HF_{\mathrm{red}}(Y,\mathfrak{s}). Altogether, we have

H​F+​(Y,𝔰)=𝒯+⊕H​Fred​(Y,𝔰).HF^{+}(Y,\mathfrak{s})=\mathcal{T}^{+}\oplus HF_{\mathrm{red}}(Y,\mathfrak{s}).

The correction term satisfies

d⁡(Y,𝔰)=d⁡(Y,J​𝔰),d⁡(−Y,𝔰)=−d⁡(Y,𝔰),d(Y,\mathfrak{s})=d(Y,J\mathfrak{s}),\qquad d(-Y,\mathfrak{s})=-d(Y,\mathfrak{s}), (2)

where J:Spinc​(Y)→Spinc​(Y)J\colon\thinspace\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y)\to\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y) is the conjugation on Spinc​(Y)\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y), and −Y-Y is YY with the orientation reversed.

2.2 Relative Spinc structures

Let MM be a compact 3–manifold with boundary consisting of tori. Let v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} be two nowhere vanishing vector fields on MM, whose restriction on each component of ∂M\partial M is the outward normal vector field. We say v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} are homologous, if they are homotopic in the complement of a ball in MM, and the homotopy is through nowhere vanishing vector fields which restrict to the outward normal vector field on ∂M\partial M. The homology classes of such vector fields are called relative Spinc structures on MM, and the set of all relative Spinc structures is denoted by Spinc¯​(M,∂M)\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(M,\partial M), which is an affine space over H2​(M,∂M)H^{2}(M,\partial M).

When KK is an oriented knot in a closed oriented 3–manifold YY, let M=Y\ν∘​(K)M=Y\backslash\overset{\circ}{\nu}(K). Then we also denote Spinc¯​(M,∂M)\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(M,\partial M) by Spinc¯​(Y,K)\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K).

Remark 2.1.

There are several different conventions in the literature for the boundary condition of vector fields representing a relative Spinc structure. In [23, 14], the restriction of the vector fields on the boundary is tangent to the boundary. Our treatment in this paper is the one taken in [24].

Suppose KK is an oriented rationally null-homologous knot in a closed manifold Y3Y^{3}, (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath${\alpha}$},\mbox{\boldmath${\beta}$},w,z) is a doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram associated to the pair (Y,K)(Y,K). There is a map

𝔰¯w,z:𝕋α∩𝕋β→Spinc¯​(Y,K),\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}\colon\thinspace\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta}\to\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K),

defined in [24]. We sketch the definition of 𝔰¯w,z\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z} as follows.

Let f:Y→[0,3]f\colon\thinspace Y\to[0,3] be a Morse function corresponding to the Heegaard diagram, ∇f\nabla f is the gradient vector field associated to ff. Let γw\gamma_{w} be the flowline of ∇f\nabla f passing through ww, which connects the index-zero critical point to the index-three critical point. Similarly, define γz\gamma_{z}. Suppose 𝐱∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta}, then 𝜸𝐱\mbox{\boldmath${\gamma}$}_{\mathbf{x}} denotes the union of the flowlines connecting index-one critical points to index-two critical points, and passing through the points in 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

We construct a nowhere vanishing vector field vv. Outside a neighborhood ν⁡(γw∪γz∪𝜸𝐱)\nu(\gamma_{w}\cup\gamma_{z}\cup\mbox{\boldmath${\gamma}$}_{\mathbf{x}}), vv is identical with ∇f\nabla f. Then one can extend vv over the balls ν⁡(𝜸𝐱)\nu(\mbox{\boldmath${\gamma}$}_{\mathbf{x}}). We can also extend vv over ν⁡(γw∪γz)\nu(\gamma_{w}\cup\gamma_{z}), so that the closed orbits of vv, which pass through ww and zz, give the oriented knot K=γz−γwK=\gamma_{z}-\gamma_{w}. There may be many different choices to extend vv over ν⁡(γw∪γz)\nu(\gamma_{w}\cup\gamma_{z}), we choose the extension as in [24, Subsection 2.4].

Now we let 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}) be the relative Spinc structure given by v|Y\ν∘​(K)v|_{Y\backslash\overset{\circ}{\nu}(K)}. It is easy to check that 𝔰¯w,z\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z} is a well-defined map.

Let uu be a vector field on S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} as described in [24, Subsection 2.2]. More precisely, uu is the inward normal vector field on the boundary torus, uu is transverse to the meridian disks in the interior of S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}, and the core of S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} is a closed orbit of uu. Given ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y,K)\xi\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K), let vv be a vector field representing ξ\xi, then we can glue vv and uu together to get a vector field on YY, which represents a Spinc structure on YY. Hence we get a map

GY,K:Spinc¯​(Y,K)→Spinc​(Y).G_{Y,K}\colon\thinspace\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K)\to\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y).

We call GY,K​(ξ)G_{Y,K}(\xi) the underlying Spinc structure of ξ\xi. It is shown in [24] that

GY,K​(𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱))=𝔰w​(𝐱).G_{Y,K}(\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}))=\mathfrak{s}_{w}(\mathbf{x}).

2.3 Knot Floer homology of rationally null-homologous knots

Suppose that KK is a rationally null-homologous knot in a closed 33–manifold YY. Let

(Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath${\alpha}$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},w,z)

be a doubly pointed Heegaard diagram for (Y,K)(Y,K). Fix a Spinc structure 𝔰\mathfrak{s} on YY and let ξ∈Spin¯c​(Y,K)\xi\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y,K) be a relative Spinc structure whose underlying Spinc structure is 𝔰\mathfrak{s}. Let C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) be an abelian group freely generated by triples [𝐱,i,j][\mathbf{x},i,j] with

𝐱∈𝕋α∩𝕋β,𝔰w​(𝐱)=𝔰\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta},\quad\mathfrak{s}_{w}(\mathbf{x})=\mathfrak{s}

and

𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)+(i−j)​P​D​[μ]=ξ.\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})+(i-j)PD[\mu]=\xi. (3)

The chain complex is endowed with the differential

∂∞[𝐱,i,j]=∑𝐲∈𝕋α∩𝕋β∑{ϕ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)|μ⁡(ϕ)=1}#⁡(ℳ^​(ϕ))​[𝐲,i−nw​(ϕ),j−nz​(ϕ)].\partial^{\infty}[\mathbf{x},i,j]=\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta}}\sum_{\{\phi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})|\mu(\phi)=1\}}\#(\widehat{\mathcal{M}}(\phi))[\mathbf{y},i-n_{w}(\phi),j-n_{z}(\phi)].

The homology of (CFK∞(Y,K,ξ),∂∞)(CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi),\partial^{\infty}) is denoted H​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)HFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi).

The grading jj gives a filtration on C​F​K0,∗​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{0,*}(Y,K,\xi), the associated graded complex is denoted C​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{CFK}(Y,K,\xi).

Given a knot KK in a rational homology sphere YY, let FF be a rational Seifert surface for KK, then there is an affine map A:Spinc¯​(Y,K)→ℚA\colon\thinspace\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K)\to\mathbb{Q} satisfying

A⁡(ξ1)−A⁡(ξ2)=⟨ξ2−ξ1,[F]⟩|[∂F]⋅[μ]|.A(\xi_{1})-A(\xi_{2})=\frac{\langle\xi_{2}-\xi_{1},[F]\rangle}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}. (4)

This map can be defined and determined by (4), once we fix the value of AA at a ξ0∈Spinc¯​(Y,K)\xi_{0}\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K) .

Let

ℬY,K={ξ∈Spinc¯(Y,K)|H​F​K^(Y,K,ξ)≠0}.\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}=\left\{\xi\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K)\left|\>\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi)\neq 0\right.\right\}.

Let

Amax=max⁡{A⁡(ξ)|ξ∈ℬY,K},Amin=min⁡{A⁡(ξ)|ξ∈ℬY,K}.A_{\max}=\max\{A(\xi)|\>\xi\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}\},\quad A_{\min}=\min\{A(\xi)|\>\xi\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}\}.

We reformulate [14, Theorem 1.1] for knots as follows.

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose KK is a knot in a rational homology sphere YY, FF is a minimal genus rational Seifert surface for KK, then

−χ⁡(F)+|[∂F]⋅[μ]||[∂F]⋅[μ]|=Amax−Amin.\frac{-\chi(F)+|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}=A_{\max}-A_{\min}.

Suppose K⊂YK\subset Y is a rationally null-homologous knot. We say that KK is rationally fibered, if the complement of KK is a surface bundle over S1S^{1}, and the fiber is a rational Seifert surface for KK.

Theorem 2.3.

Suppose K⊂YK\subset Y is a rationally null-homologous knot, FF is a rational Seifert surface for KK. Then the complement of KK fibers over S1S^{1} with fiber FF if and only if the group

⨁ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y,K),A⁡(ξ)=AmaxH​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\bigoplus_{\xi\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K),A(\xi)=A_{\max}}\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi)

is isomorphic to ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

This follows from [12], [14, Proposition 5.15], and the fact that a knot is rationally fibered if and only if any of its cables is rationally fibered. ∎

2.4 Rational domains and the relative rational bigrading

When 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a torsion Spinc structure over YY, as in Ozsváth–Szabó [20] there is an absolute ℚ\mathbb{Q}–grading on C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) and the induced complexes. Let H​F​K^d​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{HFK}_{d}(Y,K,\xi) be the summand of H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi) at the absolute grading dd.

We first recall Lee–Lipshitz’s construction of the relative ℚ\mathbb{Q}–grading [9]. Suppose D1,…,DND_{1},\dots,D_{N} are closures of the components of Σ−𝜶−𝜷\Sigma-\mbox{\boldmath${\alpha}$}-\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}, thought of as 22–chains. Suppose ψ=∑iai​Di\psi=\sum_{i}a_{i}D_{i} for some rational numbers aia_{i}, and let ∂αψ\partial_{\alpha}\psi be the intersection of ∂ψ\partial\psi with 𝜶{\alpha}, then ∂∂αψ\partial\partial_{\alpha}\psi is a rational linear combination of intersection points between α\alpha and β\beta curves. We say ψ\psi is a rational domain connecting 𝐱=(x1,…,xg)∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{g})\in\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta} to 𝐲=(y1,…,yg)∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{g})\in\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta}, if

∂∂αψ=y1+⋯+yg−(x1+⋯+xg).\partial\partial_{\alpha}\psi=y_{1}+\cdots+y_{g}-(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{g}).

If ψ=∑iai​Di\psi=\sum_{i}a_{i}D_{i} is a rational domain connecting 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y} with nw​(ψ)=0n_{w}(\psi)=0, then we define the Maslov index 11 1 Unfortunately, we use μ\mu to denote both the Maslov index of a rational domain and the meridian of a knot. This should not cause confusion in our current paper.

μ⁡(ψ)=∑iai​(e⁡(Di)+n𝐱​(Di)+n𝐲​(Di)),\mu(\psi)=\sum_{i}a_{i}\big(e(D_{i})+n_{\mathbf{x}}(D_{i})+n_{\mathbf{y}}(D_{i})\big),

where e⁡(Di)e(D_{i}) is the Euler measure of DiD_{i} as defined by Lipshitz [10].

The following lemma is contained in the last paragraph of [9, Section 2].

Lemma 2.4 (Lee–Lipshitz).

Suppose ψ\psi is a rational domain connecting 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y} with nw​(ψ)=0n_{w}(\psi)=0, then

Gr⁡(𝐱)−Gr⁡(𝐲)=μ⁡(ψ).\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{x})-\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{y})=\mu(\psi).

There is a similar formula for the relative Alexander grading.

Lemma 2.5.

Suppose ψ\psi is a rational domain connecting 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y}, then

A⁡(𝐱)−A⁡(𝐲)=nz​(ψ)−nw​(ψ).A(\mathbf{x})-A(\mathbf{y})=n_{z}(\psi)-n_{w}(\psi).
Proof.

Let FF be a rational Seifert surface for KK. By (4) and [16, Lemma 2.19],

A⁡(𝐱)−A⁡(𝐲)\displaystyle A(\mathbf{x})-A(\mathbf{y}) =\displaystyle= ⟨PD⁡[∂ψ],[F]⟩|[∂F]⋅[μ]|\displaystyle\frac{\langle\mathrm{PD}[\partial\psi],[F]\rangle}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}
=\displaystyle= [∂ψ]⋅[F]|[∂F]⋅[μ]|\displaystyle\frac{[\partial\psi]\cdot[F]}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}

which is the rational linking number between ∂ψ\partial\psi and KK. This linking number can also be computed by [ψ]⋅[K]=nz​(ψ)−nw​(ψ)[\psi]\cdot[K]=n_{z}(\psi)-n_{w}(\psi). ∎

3 Symmetries in knot Floer homology

Suppose that KK is a rationally null-homologous knot in a 33–manifold YY. Let

Γ1=(Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)\Gamma_{1}=(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath${\alpha}$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},w,z)

be a doubly pointed Heegaard diagram for (Y,K)(Y,K). Then

Γ2=(−Σ,𝜷,𝜶,z,w)\Gamma_{2}=(-\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath${\alpha}$},z,w)

is also a Heegaard diagram for (Y,K)(Y,K). We call Γ2\Gamma_{2} the dual diagram of Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Let 𝔰¯w,zi​(𝐱)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}^{i}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}) be the associated relative Spinc structure for the diagram Γi\Gamma_{i}. We define a map J~:ℬY,K→Spinc¯​(Y,K)\widetilde{J}\colon\thinspace\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}\to\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K) as follows. If

𝔰¯w,z1​(𝐱)=ξ,\underline{\mathfrak{s}}^{1}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})=\xi,

for some 𝐱\mathbf{x}, then define

J~​ξ=J~Γ1​ξ=𝔰¯z,w2​(𝐱).\widetilde{J}\xi=\widetilde{J}_{\Gamma_{1}}\xi=\underline{\mathfrak{s}}^{2}_{z,w}(\mathbf{x}).
Lemma 3.1.

The map J~\widetilde{J} does not depend on the diagram Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

Proof.

This follows from the standard procedure of proving the invariance of H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi). Suppose Γ1,Γ1′\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{1}^{\prime} are two different diagrams for (Y,K)(Y,K), then they are connected by the following types of moves:
∙\bullet isotopies of the 𝜶{\alpha} and the 𝜷{\beta} without crossing w,zw,z,
∙\bullet handleslides amongst the 𝜶{\alpha} or the 𝜷{\beta},
∙\bullet stabilizations.
Then the dual diagrams Γ2\Gamma_{2} and Γ2′\Gamma_{2}^{\prime} are also related by the corresponding moves. Tracing these moves, the proof of the invariance of H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi) implies that J~Γ1=J~Γ1′\widetilde{J}_{\Gamma_{1}}=\widetilde{J}_{\Gamma_{1}^{\prime}}. ∎

Lemma 3.2.

Suppose ξ∈ℬY,K\xi\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}, then

GY,K​(J~​ξ)=J​GY,K​(ξ)+PD⁡[K].G_{Y,K}(\widetilde{J}\xi)=JG_{Y,K}(\xi)+\mathrm{PD}[K].
Proof.

Suppose ξ=𝔰¯w,z1​(𝐱)\xi=\underline{\mathfrak{s}}^{1}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}), then GY,K​(ξ)=𝔰w1​(𝐱)G_{Y,K}(\xi)=\mathfrak{s}^{1}_{w}(\mathbf{x}), hence J​GY,K​(ξ)=𝔰w2​(𝐱)JG_{Y,K}(\xi)=\mathfrak{s}^{2}_{w}(\mathbf{x}). On the other hand, J~​ξ=𝔰¯z,w2​(𝐱)\widetilde{J}\xi=\underline{\mathfrak{s}}^{2}_{z,w}(\mathbf{x}), so GY,K​(J~​ξ)=𝔰z2​(𝐱)G_{Y,K}(\widetilde{J}\xi)=\mathfrak{s}^{2}_{z}(\mathbf{x}). By [16, Lemma 2.19] or [26, Equation (1)],

𝔰z2​(𝐱)=𝔰w2​(𝐱)+PD⁡[K].\mathfrak{s}^{2}_{z}(\mathbf{x})=\mathfrak{s}^{2}_{w}(\mathbf{x})+\mathrm{PD}[K].

So our conclusion holds. ∎

The following theorem is an analogue of [20, Proposition 3.10]. We have been informed that some cases of the theorem are already contained in [1].

Theorem 3.3.

Let 𝔰\mathfrak{s} be a Spinc structure over YY, and let ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y,K)\xi\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K) be a relative Spinc structure with underlying Spinc structure 𝔰\mathfrak{s}.

(a) There is an isomorphism of chain complexes

C​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)≅C​F​K^​(Y,K,J~​ξ).\widehat{CFK}(Y,K,\xi)\cong\widehat{CFK}(Y,K,\widetilde{J}\xi).

(b) The map J~\widetilde{J} maps ℬY,K\mathcal{B}_{Y,K} into ℬY,K\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}, and J~2=id\widetilde{J}^{2}=\mathrm{id}.

(c) If 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a torsion Spinc structure, then there is an isomorphism of absolutely graded chain complexes:

C​F​K^∗​(Y,K,ξ)≅C​F​K^∗+d​(Y,K,J~​ξ),\widehat{CFK}_{*}(Y,K,\xi)\cong\widehat{CFK}_{*+d}(Y,K,\widetilde{J}\xi),

where d=A⁡(J~​ξ)−A⁡(ξ)d=A(\widetilde{J}\xi)-A(\xi).

Proof.

(a) If ϕ\phi is a holomorphic disk in Γ1\Gamma_{1} connecting 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y}, then ϕ\phi gives rise to a holomorphic disk ϕ¯\overline{\phi} in Γ2\Gamma_{2} connecting 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y}. Topologically, ϕ¯\overline{\phi} is just −ϕ-\phi.

The above argument implies that C​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)≅C​F​K^​(Y,K,J~​ξ)\widehat{CFK}(Y,K,\xi)\cong\widehat{CFK}(Y,K,\widetilde{J}\xi) as chain complexes.

(b) The isomorphism in (a) implies that J~\widetilde{J} maps ℬY,K\mathcal{B}_{Y,K} into ℬY,K\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}.

If ξ∈ℬY,K\xi\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K} is represented by 𝐱\mathbf{x} in Γ1\Gamma_{1}, then J~​ξ∈ℬY,K\widetilde{J}\xi\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K} is represented by 𝐱\mathbf{x} in Γ2\Gamma_{2}. Using Lemma 3.1, J~2​ξ=J~Γ2​J~​ξ\widetilde{J}^{2}\xi=\widetilde{J}_{\Gamma_{2}}\widetilde{J}\xi is represented by 𝐱\mathbf{x} in Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

(c) Since 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is torsion, there exists an absolute ℚ\mathbb{Q}–grading on C​F^​(Y,𝔰)\widehat{CF}(Y,\mathfrak{s}), hence an induced absolute ℚ\mathbb{Q}–grading on C​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{CFK}(Y,K,\xi). Since the isomorphism in (a) preserves the relative grading, there exists a rational number dd, such that

C​F​K^∗​(Y,K,ξ)≅C​F​K^∗+d​(Y,K,J~​ξ).\widehat{CFK}_{*}(Y,K,\xi)\cong\widehat{CFK}_{*+d}(Y,K,\widetilde{J}\xi).

It is clear that the number dd does not depend on the choice of the Heegaard diagram, because both H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi) and H​F​K^​(Y,K,J~​ξ)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\widetilde{J}\xi) are nontrivial absolutely graded groups.

Using (a), we get two isomorphisms which increase the Maslov grading by dd:

g1:C​F​K^​(Γ1,ξ)→C​F​K^​(Γ2,J~​ξ),g_{1}\colon\thinspace\widehat{CFK}(\Gamma_{1},\xi)\to\widehat{CFK}(\Gamma_{2},\widetilde{J}\xi),
g2:C​F​K^​(Γ2,ξ)→C​F​K^​(Γ1,J~​ξ).g_{2}\colon\thinspace\widehat{CFK}(\Gamma_{2},\xi)\to\widehat{CFK}(\Gamma_{1},\widetilde{J}\xi).

Since both Γ1\Gamma_{1} and Γ2\Gamma_{2} represent (Y,K)(Y,K), there is a grading preserving chain homotopy equivalence

f:C​F​K^​(Γ1,ξ)→C​F​K^​(Γ2,ξ).f\colon\thinspace\widehat{CFK}(\Gamma_{1},\xi)\to\widehat{CFK}(\Gamma_{2},\xi).

Suppose 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} in Γ1\Gamma_{1} is a generator for C​F​K^​(Γ1,ξ)\widehat{CFK}(\Gamma_{1},\xi), let 𝐱2=g1​(𝐱1)\mathbf{x}_{2}=g_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}) in Γ2\Gamma_{2}. Let 𝐲2\mathbf{y}_{2} in Γ2\Gamma_{2} be a generator which contributes to f⁡(𝐱1)f(\mathbf{x}_{1}), and let 𝐲1=g2​(𝐲2)\mathbf{y}_{1}=g_{2}(\mathbf{y}_{2}) in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Since g1,g2g_{1},g_{2} increase the grading by dd and ff is grading preserving, we have

Gr⁡(𝐱1)=Gr⁡(𝐲2)=Gr⁡(𝐲1)−d=Gr⁡(𝐱2)−d.\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{x}_{1})=\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{y}_{2})=\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{y}_{1})-d=\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{x}_{2})-d. (5)

Since 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is torsion and [K][K] is rationally null-homologous, J​𝔰+PD⁡[K]J\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K] is also torsion. Using Lemma 3.2, we conclude that there exists a rational domain ψ1\psi_{1} in Γ1\Gamma_{1} connecting 𝐲1\mathbf{y}_{1} to 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1}, such that nw​(ψ1)=0n_{w}(\psi_{1})=0. By Lemma 2.4 and (5), we see that

μ⁡(ψ1)=Gr⁡(𝐲1)−Gr⁡(𝐱1)=d.\mu(\psi_{1})=\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{y}_{1})-\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{x}_{1})=d. (6)

Moreover, by Lemma 2.5

nz​(ψ1)=A⁡(𝐲1)−A⁡(𝐱1)=A⁡(J~​ξ)−A⁡(ξ).n_{z}(\psi_{1})=A(\mathbf{y}_{1})-A(\mathbf{x}_{1})=A(\widetilde{J}\xi)-A(\xi). (7)

Noting that ψ2=(−ψ1)−nz​(ψ1)​(−Σ)\psi_{2}=(-\psi_{1})-n_{z}(\psi_{1})(-\Sigma) is a rational domain in Γ2\Gamma_{2} that connects 𝐲2\mathbf{y}_{2} to 𝐱2\mathbf{x}_{2} with nz​(ψ2)=0n_{z}(\psi_{2})=0, and that μ⁡(−Σ)=2\mu(-\Sigma)=2 in Γ2\Gamma_{2}, we have

Gr⁡(𝐲2)−Gr⁡(𝐱2)=μ⁡(ψ2)=μ⁡(ψ1)−2​nz​(ψ1).\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{y}_{2})-\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{x}_{2})=\mu(\psi_{2})=\mu(\psi_{1})-2n_{z}(\psi_{1}). (8)

It follows from (6), (8) and (5) that

μ⁡(ψ1)+(μ⁡(ψ1)−2​nz​(ψ1))=0.\mu(\psi_{1})+(\mu(\psi_{1})-2n_{z}(\psi_{1}))=0.

Hence

μ⁡(ψ1)=nz​(ψ1),\mu(\psi_{1})=n_{z}(\psi_{1}),

so it follows from (6) and (7) that d=A⁡(J~​ξ)−A⁡(ξ)d=A(\widetilde{J}\xi)-A(\xi). ∎

For any 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y), let

H​F​K^​(Y,K,𝔰)=⨁ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y,K),GY,K​(ξ)=𝔰H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ).\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\mathfrak{s})=\bigoplus_{\xi\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K),\>G_{Y,K}(\xi)=\mathfrak{s}}\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi).
Corollary 3.4.

Suppose KK is a rationally null-homologous knot in YY, 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a Spinc structure over YY. Then there is an isomorphism

ι:H​F​K^​(Y,K,𝔰)≅H​F​K^​(Y,K,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K]).\iota\colon\thinspace\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\mathfrak{s})\cong\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,J\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K]).

If 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is torsion, and ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y,K)∈GY,K−1​(𝔰)\xi\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K)\in G_{Y,K}^{-1}(\mathfrak{s}), then the restriction of ι\iota on H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi) is homogeneous of degree A⁡(J~​ξ)−A⁡(ξ)A(\widetilde{J}\xi)-A(\xi).

Proof.

This follows from Theorem 3.3 and Lemma 3.2. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Suppose ξ1,ξ2∈ℬY,K\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}, then

J~​ξ1−J~​ξ2=−(ξ1−ξ2)∈H2​(Y,K).\widetilde{J}\xi_{1}-\widetilde{J}\xi_{2}=-(\xi_{1}-\xi_{2})\in H^{2}(Y,K).
Proof.

Suppose ξ1,ξ2\xi_{1},\xi_{2} are represented by intersection points 𝐱,𝐲\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}. Let aa be a multi α\alpha arc connecting 𝐲\mathbf{y} to 𝐱\mathbf{x}, bb be a multi β\beta arc connecting 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y}. By [16, Lemma 2.19], ξ1−ξ2\xi_{1}-\xi_{2} is represented by a+ba+b, and J~​ξ1−J~​ξ2\widetilde{J}\xi_{1}-\widetilde{J}\xi_{2} is represented by (−b)+(−a)(-b)+(-a). So our conclusion holds. ∎

Corollary 3.6.

Suppose ξ∈ℬY,K\xi\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}, then A⁡(ξ)=AmaxA(\xi)=A_{\max} if and only if A⁡(J~​ξ)=AminA(\widetilde{J}\xi)=A_{\min}.

Proof.

If A⁡(ξ)≥A⁡(η)A(\xi)\geq A(\eta) for all η∈ℬY,K\eta\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}, then Lemma 3.5 shows that A⁡(J~​ξ)≤A⁡(J~​η)A(\widetilde{J}\xi)\leq A(\widetilde{J}\eta) for all η∈ℬY,K\eta\in\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}. Since J~\widetilde{J} surjects onto ℬY,K\mathcal{B}_{Y,K}, A⁡(J~​ξ)=AminA(\widetilde{J}\xi)=A_{\min}. ∎

If we choose the affine map AA such that Amax=−AminA_{\max}=-A_{\min}, then the above corollary implies that A⁡(J~​ξ)=−A⁡(ξ)A(\widetilde{J}\xi)=-A(\xi).

4 A lower bound for Θ\Theta

In this section, we will prove Theorem 1.1. For simplicity, we will work over a fixed field 𝔽\mathbb{F}. (A priori, the correction terms defined over different fields may not be the same, but they have similar properties. When 𝔽=ℚ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Q}, the correction terms are the same as the original correction terms defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}.)

4.1 Computing correction terms from C​F​K∞CFK^{\infty}

Fix a doubly pointed Heegaard diagram Γ1=(Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)\Gamma_{1}=(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath${\alpha}$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},w,z) and consider the associated knot Floer chain complex C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) with GY,K​(ξ)=𝔰G_{Y,K}(\xi)=\mathfrak{s}. Recall that C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) is an abelian group freely generated by triples [𝐲,i,j][\mathbf{y},i,j] with

𝐲∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta}

and

𝔰¯w,z​(𝐲)+(i−j)​P​D​[μ]=ξ.\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{y})+(i-j)PD[\mu]=\xi.

Let 𝔊=𝔊Y,K\mathfrak{G}=\mathfrak{G}_{Y,K} be a set of generators of H​F​K^​(Y,K)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K), such that each generator is supported in a single relative Spinc structure and a single Maslov grading. By [25, Lemma 4.5], C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) is homotopy equivalent to a chain complex whose underlying abelian group is H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ)⊗𝔽⁡[U,U−1]\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi)\otimes\mathbb{F}[U,U^{-1}], so we may assume C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) is generated by generators [𝐱,i,j][\mathbf{x},i,j] satisfying that every 𝐱\mathbf{x} is in 𝔊\mathfrak{G}.

Since YY is a rational homology sphere, H​F∞​(Y,𝔰)≅𝔽⁡[U,U−1]HF^{\infty}(Y,\mathfrak{s})\cong\mathbb{F}[U,U^{-1}]. Fix a sufficiently large integer NN. Let 𝒢𝔰⊂C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}\subset CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) be the set that consists of all homogeneous chains that represent U−N∈H​F∞​(Y,𝔰)U^{-N}\in HF^{\infty}(Y,\mathfrak{s}):

𝒢𝔰={X=∑𝐱∈𝔊,i,j∈ℤa𝐱,i,j[𝐱,i,j]|[X]=U−N∈HF∞(Y,𝔰),Gr[𝐱,i,j]=d(Y,𝔰)+2N}\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}=\left\{X=\left.\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathfrak{G},i,j\in\mathbb{Z}}a_{\mathbf{x},i,j}[\mathbf{x},i,j]\,\right|\,[X]=U^{-N}\in HF^{\infty}(Y,\mathfrak{s}),\mathrm{Gr}[\mathbf{x},i,j]=d(Y,\mathfrak{s})+2N\right\}

where Gr\mathrm{Gr} is the absolute Maslov grading.

Lemma 4.1.

With the above notation,

N=minX∈𝒢𝔰⁡max[𝐱,i,j]∈X​i.N=\min_{X\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}}\max_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}i.

Proposition 4.2.

With the same assumption,

d⁡(Y,𝔰)=maxX∈𝒢𝔰⁡min[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡Gr⁡(𝐱).d(Y,{\mathfrak{s}})=\max_{X\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}}\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}(\mathbf{x}). (9)

∎

4.2 More symmetries

Recall that the chain complex C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) can be viewed at the same time as C​F​K∞​(Y,K,J~​ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\widetilde{J}\xi) associated to the Heegaard diagram

Γ2=(−Σ,𝜷,𝜶,z,w).\Gamma_{2}=(-\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath${\alpha}$},z,w).

There is a natural identification between intersection points in Γ1\Gamma_{1} and Γ2\Gamma_{2}, and this can be extended to a chain isomorphism f:C​F​KΓ1∞​(Y,K)→C​F​KΓ2∞​(Y,K)f\colon\thinspace CFK^{\infty}_{\Gamma_{1}}(Y,K)\rightarrow CFK^{\infty}_{\Gamma_{2}}(Y,K) given by f⁡([𝐱,i,j])=[𝐱,j,i]f([\mathbf{x},i,j])=[\mathbf{x},j,i], where 𝐱∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb{T}_{\beta}, and i,j∈ℤi,j\in\mathbb{Z} denote the filtration with respect to w,zw,z respectively.

Lemma 4.3.

Under the isomorphism ff, the set 𝒢𝔰\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}} is identified with the set of all homogeneous generators that represent U−M∈H​F∞​(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])U^{-M}\in HF^{\infty}(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K]) for some large integer MM, associated to the Heegaard diagram Γ2\Gamma_{2}.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.2, the map

f:C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)→C​F​K∞​(Y,K,J~​ξ)f\colon\thinspace CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi)\rightarrow CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\widetilde{J}\xi)

descends to

f:C​F∞​(Y,𝔰)→C​F∞​(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K]).f\colon\thinspace CF^{\infty}(Y,{\mathfrak{s}})\rightarrow CF^{\infty}(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K]).

Moreover, since ff is a chain isomorphism, each element of f⁡(𝒢𝔰)f(\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}) must represent a certain generator U−M∈H​F∞​(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])U^{-M}\in HF^{\infty}(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K]) for some MM.

Finally, we need to prove that the elements in f⁡(𝒢𝔰)f(\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}) are homogeneous. Let Grk\mathrm{Gr}_{k} denote the grading pertaining to the Heegaard diagram Γk\Gamma_{k}. Suppose [𝐱1,i1,j1][\mathbf{x}_{1},i_{1},j_{1}] and [𝐱2,i2,j2][\mathbf{x}_{2},i_{2},j_{2}] contribute to X=∑a𝐱,i,j​[𝐱,i,j]∈𝒢𝔰X=\sum a_{\mathbf{x},i,j}[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}, then Gr1​([𝐱1,i1,j1])=Gr1​([𝐱2,i2,j2])\mathrm{Gr}_{1}([\mathbf{x}_{1},i_{1},j_{1}])=\mathrm{Gr}_{1}([\mathbf{x}_{2},i_{2},j_{2}]). Since 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} and 𝐱2\mathbf{x}_{2} belong to the same Spinc structure, there exists a topological disk ϕ\phi in Γ1\Gamma_{1} connecting them. By adding an appropriate multiple of Σ\Sigma, we may further assume that nw​(ϕ)=i1−i2n_{w}(\phi)=i_{1}-i_{2}. Thus, μ⁡(ϕ)=0\mu(\phi)=0 according to the Maslov index formula. Moreover, since [𝐱1,i1,j1][\mathbf{x}_{1},i_{1},j_{1}] and [𝐱2,i2,j2][\mathbf{x}_{2},i_{2},j_{2}] satisfy (3), we have

𝔰¯w,z1​(𝐱1)+(i1−j1)​P​D​[μ]=𝔰¯w,z1​(𝐱2)+(i2−j2)​P​D​[μ],\underline{\mathfrak{s}}^{1}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}_{1})+(i_{1}-j_{1})PD[\mu]=\underline{\mathfrak{s}}^{1}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}_{2})+(i_{2}-j_{2})PD[\mu],

which implies that (as in Lemma 2.5)

nz​(ϕ)−nw​(ϕ)+(i1−j1)=(i2−j2).n_{z}(\phi)-n_{w}(\phi)+(i_{1}-j_{1})=(i_{2}-j_{2}).

So nz​(ϕ)=j1−j2n_{z}(\phi)=j_{1}-j_{2}. Consequently, the disk −ϕ-\phi connects [𝐱1,i1,j1][\mathbf{x}_{1},i_{1},j_{1}] and [𝐱2,i2,j2][\mathbf{x}_{2},i_{2},j_{2}] in the Heegaard diagram Γ2\Gamma_{2}. As the Maslov index of ϕ\phi is invariant under the reversion of orientation,

Gr2​([𝐱1,j1,i1])−Gr2​([𝐱2,j2,i2])=μ⁡(ϕ)=0.\mathrm{Gr}_{2}([\mathbf{x}_{1},j_{1},i_{1}])-\mathrm{Gr}_{2}([\mathbf{x}_{2},j_{2},i_{2}])=\mu(\phi)=0.

This proved the elements in f⁡(𝒢𝔰)f(\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}) are homogeneous in Gr2\mathrm{Gr}_{2}. ∎

Applying Lemma 4.1 to f⁡(𝒢𝔰)f(\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}), the set of homogeneous generators that represent U−M∈H​F∞​(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])U^{-M}\in HF^{\infty}(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K]), we conclude:

M=minX∈𝒢𝔰⁡max[𝐱,i,j]∈X​j.M=\min_{X\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}}\max_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}j.

With the same argument as in Proposition 4.2, this leads to the following analogous correction term formula.

d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])=maxX∈𝒢𝔰⁡min[𝐱,i,j]∈X​Gr2​(𝐱).d(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K])=\max_{X\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}}\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x}). (10)

4.3 Proof of Theorem 1.1

Our proof is based on the following elementary principle.

Lemma 4.4.

For any bounded sequence of pairs (ai,bi)∈(a,b)+ℤ2(a_{i},b_{i})\in(a,b)+\mathbb{Z}^{2}, where (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, we have

|mini⁡ai−mini⁡bi|≤maxi⁡|ai−bi|,|\min_{i}a_{i}-\min_{i}b_{i}|\leq\max_{i}|a_{i}-b_{i}|,
|maxi⁡ai−maxi⁡bi|≤maxi⁡|ai−bi|.|\max_{i}a_{i}-\max_{i}b_{i}|\leq\max_{i}|a_{i}-b_{i}|.
Proof.

The condition that (ai,bi)∈(a,b)+ℤ2(a_{i},b_{i})\in(a,b)+\mathbb{Z}^{2} is bounded allows us to take minimum and maximum. Assume a=am=mini⁡aia=a_{m}=\min_{i}a_{i} and b=bk=mini⁡bib=b_{k}=\min_{i}b_{i}. Then,

a−b=am−bk≤ak−bk;a-b=a_{m}-b_{k}\leq a_{k}-b_{k};

and

b−a=bk−am≤bm−am.b-a=b_{k}-a_{m}\leq b_{m}-a_{m}.

It readily follow that

|a−b|≤maxi⁡|ai−bi|.|a-b|\leq\max_{i}|a_{i}-b_{i}|.

The second inequality follows from the first by replacing ai,bia_{i},b_{i} with −ai,−bi-a_{i},-b_{i}. ∎

To bound |d⁡(Y,𝔰)−d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])||d(Y,{\mathfrak{s}})-d(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K])|, we apply Lemma 4.4 twice to the equations (9) and (10). In the first round, let the pair

(aX,bX)=(min[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡Gr1​(𝐱),min[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡Gr2​(𝐱))(a_{X},b_{X})=\Big(\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x})\Big)

and X∈𝒢𝔰X\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}} be the index of the sequence. We get

|d⁡(Y,𝔰)−d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])|≤maxX∈𝒢𝔰⁡|min[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡Gr1​(𝐱)−min[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡Gr2​(𝐱)|.\Big|d(Y,{\mathfrak{s}})-d(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K])\Big|\leq\max_{X\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{s}}}\Big|\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x})\Big|.

In the second round, let the pair

(a𝐱,b𝐱)=(Gr1​(𝐱),Gr2​(𝐱))(a_{\mathbf{x}},b_{\mathbf{x}})=\left(\mathrm{Gr}_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x})\right)

and 𝐱∈𝔊\mathbf{x}\in\mathfrak{G} be the index of the sequence. We get

|min[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡Gr1​(𝐱)−min[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡Gr2​(𝐱)|≤max[𝐱,i,j]∈X⁡|Gr1​(𝐱)−Gr2​(𝐱)|.\Big|\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-\min_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x})\Big|\leq\max_{[\mathbf{x},i,j]\in X}\Big|\mathrm{Gr}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x})\Big|.

Plugging the second inequality to the first, we obtain:

|d⁡(Y,𝔰)−d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])|≤max𝐱∈𝔊⁡|Gr1​(𝐱)−Gr2​(𝐱)|.|d(Y,{\mathfrak{s}})-d(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K])|\leq\max_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathfrak{G}}|\mathrm{Gr}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x})|. (11)

The proof of Theorem 3.3 (b) implies that

Gr2​(𝐱)−Gr1​(𝐱)=A⁡(J~​𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱))−A⁡(𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)).\mathrm{Gr}_{2}(\mathbf{x})-\mathrm{Gr}_{1}(\mathbf{x})=A(\widetilde{J}\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}))-A(\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})).

Recall that at the beginning of this section, we assumed that H​F​K^​(Y,K)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K) was generated by 𝐱∈𝔊\mathbf{x}\in\mathfrak{G}, Theorem 2.2 then implies that the right hand side of (11) is bounded from above by the left hand side of (1). So (11) implies

|d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])−d⁡(Y,𝔰)|≤1+−χ⁡(F)|[∂F]⋅[μ]|.|d(Y,J{\mathfrak{s}}+\mathrm{PD}[K])-d(Y,{\mathfrak{s}})|\leq 1+\frac{-\chi(F)}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}.

By (2), d⁡(Y,𝔰)=d⁡(Y,J​𝔰)d(Y,\mathfrak{s})=d(Y,J\mathfrak{s}). So we get

1+−χ⁡(F)|[∂F]⋅[μ]|\displaystyle 1+\frac{-\chi(F)}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|} ≥\displaystyle\geq max𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)⁡{d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])−d⁡(Y,J​𝔰)}\displaystyle\max_{\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y)}\big\{d(Y,J\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K])-d(Y,J\mathfrak{s})\big\}
=\displaystyle= max𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)⁡{d⁡(Y,𝔰+PD⁡[K])−d⁡(Y,𝔰)}.\displaystyle\max_{\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y)}\big\{d(Y,\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K])-d(Y,\mathfrak{s})\big\}.

This finishes the proof of Theorem 1.1.

5 Applications

In this section, we apply Theorem 1.1 to compute Θ\Theta for certain homology classes in two types of manifolds: L-spaces and large surgeries on knots in S3S^{3}.

5.1 Floer simple knots in L-spaces

Proposition 5.1.

Suppose YY is an L-space, KK is a Floer simple knot in YY, FF is a genus minimizing rational Seifert surface for KK. Then the Euler characteristic of FF is determined by the formula

1+−χ⁡(F)|[∂F]⋅[μ]|=max𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)⁡{d⁡(Y,𝔰+PD⁡[K])−d⁡(Y,𝔰)}.1+\frac{-\chi(F)}{|[\partial F]\cdot[\mu]|}=\max_{\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y)}\big\{d(Y,\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K])-d(Y,\mathfrak{s})\big\}. (12)
Proof.

As in the proof of Theorem 1.1, the right hand side of (12) is equal to

max𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)⁡{d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])−d⁡(Y,𝔰)}.\max_{\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y)}\big\{d(Y,J\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K])-d(Y,\mathfrak{s})\big\}.

As YY is an L-space and KK is Floer simple, for any 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y), there exists a ξ𝔰∈Spinc¯​(Y,K)\xi_{\mathfrak{s}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,K) such that

H​F​K^​(Y,K,ξ𝔰)≅H​F​K^​(Y,K,𝔰)≅H​F^​(Y,𝔰)≅ℤ.\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\xi_{\mathfrak{s}})\cong\widehat{HFK}(Y,K,\mathfrak{s})\cong\widehat{HF}(Y,\mathfrak{s})\cong\mathbb{Z}.

Corollary 3.4 implies that J~​ξ𝔰=ξJ​𝔰+PD⁡[K]\widetilde{J}\xi_{\mathfrak{s}}=\xi_{J\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K]}, and

A⁡(J~​ξ𝔰)−A⁡(ξ𝔰)=d⁡(Y,J​𝔰+PD⁡[K])−d⁡(Y,𝔰).A(\widetilde{J}\xi_{\mathfrak{s}})-A(\xi_{\mathfrak{s}})=d(Y,J\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[K])-d(Y,\mathfrak{s}).

Since H​F​K^​(Y,K)\widehat{HFK}(Y,K) is supported in these ξ𝔰\xi_{\mathfrak{s}}’s, our conclusion follows from Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 3.6. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

This follows from Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 5.1. ∎

Proposition 5.2.

Suppose KK is a Floer simple knot in an L-space YY. Then KK is a rationally fibered knot if and only if the right hand side of (12) is achieved by exactly one 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y).

Proof.

This follows from Theorem 2.3, Corollary 3.6 and the proof of Proposition 5.1. ∎

Corollary 5.3.

Suppose K1,K2K_{1},K_{2} are two Floer simple knots in an L-space YY with [K1]=[K2]∈H1​(Y,ℤ)[K_{1}]=[K_{2}]\in H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z}), then K1K_{1} and K2K_{2} have the same rational genus, and K1K_{1} is rationally fibered if and only if K2K_{2} is rationally fibered.

Proof.

This follows from Propositions 5.1 and 5.2 by observing that the right hand side of (12) only depends on the homology class [K][K]. ∎

5.2 Large surgeries on knots

In this subsection, we will consider another case of the rational genus bound. Suppose that KK is a knot in a homology sphere YY. Let Yp​(K)Y_{p}(K) be the manifold obtained by pp–surgery on KK, and let K′⊂Yp​(K)K^{\prime}\subset Y_{p}(K) be the dual knot of the surgery. We can isotope K′K^{\prime} to be a curve on ∂ν⁡(K′)=∂ν⁡(K)\partial\nu(K^{\prime})=\partial\nu(K) such that this curve is isotopic to the meridian μ\mu of KK. We always orient K′K^{\prime} such that the orientation coincides with the standard orientation on μ\mu. If FF is a Seifert surface for KK, then FF (or −F-F if one cares about the orientation) is also a rational Seifert surface for K′K^{\prime}. So 2​g​(K)−1p\frac{2g(K)-1}{p} is an upper bound for Θ⁡([K′])\Theta([K^{\prime}]). Theorem 1.1 gives a lower bound for Θ⁡([K′])\Theta([K^{\prime}]), which we will compute.

The set of Spinc structures Spinc​(Yp​(K))\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y_{p}(K)) is in one-to-one correspondence with H2​(Yp​(K))≅ℤ/p​ℤH^{2}(Y_{p}(K))\cong\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}. However, this correspondence is generally not canonical. Ozsváth and Szabó [20] specified an identification of Spinc​(Yp​(K))\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y_{p}(K)) with ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} as follows. Let F⊂YF\subset Y be a Seifert surface for KK, W:Yp​(K)→YW\colon\thinspace Y_{p}(K)\to Y be the 22–handle cobordism, and F^⊂W\widehat{F}\subset W be the surface obtained from FF by capping off ∂F\partial F with the cocore of the 22–handle. For any i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, let 𝔵i∈Spinc​(W)\mathfrak{x}_{i}\in\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(W) be the Spinc structure satisfying that

⟨c1​(𝔵i),[F^]⟩=2​i−p.\langle c_{1}(\mathfrak{x}_{i}),[\widehat{F}]\rangle=2i-p.

Now we define a map σ:Spinc​(Yp​(K))→ℤ/p​ℤ\sigma\colon\thinspace\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y_{p}(K))\to\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} by

σ⁡(𝔵i|Yp​(K))≡i(modp).\sigma(\mathfrak{x}_{i}|Y_{p}(K))\equiv i\pmod{p}.

This map is well-defined, and is the identification we want.

By [18], the Spinc cobordism (W,𝔵i):(Yp​(K),i)→Y(W,\mathfrak{x}_{i})\colon\thinspace(Y_{p}(K),i)\to Y induces an isomorphism

F(W,𝔵i)∞:H​F∞​(Yp​(K),i)→H​F∞​(Y),F^{\infty}_{(W,\mathfrak{x}_{i})}\colon\thinspace HF^{\infty}(Y_{p}(K),i)\to HF^{\infty}(Y),

which shifts the grading by −(2​i−p)2+p4​p\frac{-(2i-p)^{2}+p}{4p}. Using the definition of correction terms, we see that

d⁡(Y)−d⁡(Yp​(K),i)≡−(2​i−p)2+p4​p(mod2).d(Y)-d(Y_{p}(K),i)\equiv\frac{-(2i-p)^{2}+p}{4p}\pmod{2}. (13)

When YY is an L-space, there is a more precise formula relating d⁡(Y)d(Y) and d​(Yp​(K),i)d(Y_{p}(K),i) in [15], which we briefly describe below. From C​F​K∞​(Y,K)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K), one can define two sequences of nonnegative integers Vk,HkV_{k},H_{k}, k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} satisfying that

Vk=H−k,Vk≥Vk+1≥Vk−1,Vg⁡(K)=0.V_{k}=H_{-k},\quad V_{k}\geq V_{k+1}\geq V_{k}-1,\quad V_{g(K)}=0. (14)

When YY is an L-space, the correction terms of Yp​(K)Y_{p}(K) can be computed by the formula

d⁡(Yp​(K),i)=d⁡(Y)+d⁡(L⁡(p,1),i)−2​max​{Vi,Hi−p}.d(Y_{p}(K),i)=d(Y)+d(L(p,1),i)-2\max\{V_{i},H_{i-p}\}. (15)

From [19] we know that

d⁡(L⁡(p,1),i)=(2​i−p)2−p4​pd(L(p,1),i)=\frac{(2i-p)^{2}-p}{4p} (16)

when 0≤i≤p0\leq i\leq p. Using (15), when 0≤i<p0\leq i<p, we get

d⁡(Yp​(K),i+1)−d⁡(Yp​(K),i)\displaystyle d(Y_{p}(K),i+1)-d(Y_{p}(K),i)
=\displaystyle= (2​i+2−p)2−p4​p−2​max​{Vi+1,Hi+1−p}−((2​i−p)2−p4​p−2​max​{Vi,Hi−p})\displaystyle\frac{(2i+2-p)^{2}-p}{4p}-2\max\{V_{i+1},H_{i+1-p}\}-\left(\frac{(2i-p)^{2}-p}{4p}-2\max\{V_{i},H_{i-p}\}\right)
=\displaystyle= 2​i+1−pp−2​max​{Vi+1,Vp−1−i}+2​max​{Vi,Vp−i}.\displaystyle\frac{2i+1-p}{p}-2\max\{V_{i+1},V_{p-1-i}\}+2\max\{V_{i},V_{p-i}\}.

Applying Theorem 1.1, we see that Θ⁡([K′])\Theta([K^{\prime}]) is bounded from below by

maxi∈{0,1,…,p−1}⁡{2​i+1−2​pp−2​max​{Vi+1,Vp−1−i}+2​max​{Vi,Vp−i}}.\max_{i\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}}\left\{\frac{2i+1-2p}{p}-2\max\{V_{i+1},V_{p-1-i}\}+2\max\{V_{i},V_{p-i}\}\right\}. (17)

The bound given by (17) is not always sharp, as there are nontrivial knots with Vk=0V_{k}=0 whenever k≥0k\geq 0. In this case the result of (17) is −1p-\frac{1}{p}. However, we can still compute Θ⁡([K′])\Theta([K^{\prime}]) for large surgeries on knots in S3S^{3}.

Lemma 5.4.

Suppose that Y,ZY,Z are two homology spheres, and K⊂YK\subset Y and L⊂ZL\subset Z are two knots. Let pp be a positive integer, K′⊂Yp​(K)K^{\prime}\subset Y_{p}(K) and L′⊂Zp​(L)L^{\prime}\subset Z_{p}(L) be the dual knots of the surgeries. If there is an orientation preserving homeomorphism f:Yp​(K)→Zp​(L)f\colon\thinspace Y_{p}(K)\to Z_{p}(L) with f∗​[K′]=[L′]f_{*}[K^{\prime}]=[L^{\prime}], then the induced map on the Spinc structures

f⋆:Spinc​(Yp​(K))→Spinc​(Zp​(L))f_{\star}\colon\thinspace\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y_{p}(K))\to\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Z_{p}(L))

is given by the identity map of ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

From the identification Spinc​(Yp​(K))≅ℤ/p​ℤ\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y_{p}(K))\cong\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} described before, we can conclude that the conjugation JJ on Spinc​(Yp​(K))\mathrm{Spin}^{c}(Y_{p}(K)) is given by

J⁡(i)≡−i(modp).J(i)\equiv-i\pmod{p}.

Since ff is a homeomorphism, one should have

f⋆​J=J​f⋆.f_{\star}J=Jf_{\star}. (18)

Moreover, the homology class [K′][K^{\prime}] corresponds to 1∈H1​(Yp​(K))≅ℤ/p​ℤ1\in H_{1}(Y_{p}(K))\cong\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, and a similar result is true for [L′][L^{\prime}]. Since f∗​[K′]=[L′]f_{*}[K^{\prime}]=[L^{\prime}], f⋆f_{\star} should satisfy

f⋆​(i+1)−f⋆​(i)=1.f_{\star}(i+1)-f_{\star}(i)=1. (19)

When pp is odd, the only affine isomorphism on ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} satisfying (18) and (19) is the identity, so our conclusion holds in this case.

When p=2​np=2n is even, the affine isomorphisms satisfying (18) and (19) are the identity and i↦i+p2i\mapsto i+\frac{p}{2}, we only need to show that the latter case cannot happen. Otherwise, we should have

d⁡(Yp​(K),i)=d⁡(Zp​(L),i+n),i∈ℤ/(2​n​ℤ).d(Y_{p}(K),i)=d(Z_{p}(L),i+n),\quad i\in\mathbb{Z}/(2n\mathbb{Z}).

By (13), we get

d⁡(Y)+2​(i−n)2−n4​n≡d⁡(Z)+2​i2−n4​n(mod2),when ​0≤i≤n.d(Y)+\frac{2(i-n)^{2}-n}{4n}\equiv d(Z)+\frac{2i^{2}-n}{4n}\pmod{2},\quad\text{when }0\leq i\leq n.

So

d⁡(Y)−d⁡(Z)≡i−n2(mod2),when ​0≤i≤n.d(Y)-d(Z)\equiv i-\frac{n}{2}\pmod{2},\quad\text{when }0\leq i\leq n. (20)

Noting that the correction term of a homology sphere is always an even integer, so the right hand side of (20) is even for any i=0,…,ni=0,\dots,n, which is impossible. ∎

Proof of Proposition 1.5.

If K′K^{\prime} is not genus minimizing, then there exists a knot L′⊂Sp3​(K)L^{\prime}\subset S^{3}_{p}(K) with [L′]=[K′][L^{\prime}]=[K^{\prime}] and ‖L′‖<‖K′‖||L^{\prime}||<||K^{\prime}||. There is a natural isomorphism H1​(∂ν⁡(L′))≅H1​(∂ν⁡(K′))H_{1}(\partial\nu(L^{\prime}))\cong H_{1}(\partial\nu(K^{\prime})). Let μL\mu_{L} be the slope on L′L^{\prime} corresponding to the meridian of KK under the previous isomorphism. Let ZZ be the manifold obtained from Sp3​(K)S^{3}_{p}(K) by μL\mu_{L}–surgery on L′L^{\prime}, and let LL be the dual knot. Then it is elementary to check that ZZ is a homology sphere, Sp3​(K)=Zp​(L)S^{3}_{p}(K)=Z_{p}(L) and g⁡(L)<g⁡(K)g(L)<g(K).

By Lemma 5.4, we have

H​F+​(Sp3​(K),i)≅H​F+​(Zp​(L),i),for any ​i∈ℤ/p​ℤ.HF^{+}(S^{3}_{p}(K),i)\cong HF^{+}(Z_{p}(L),i),\quad\text{for any }i\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}. (21)

Since p>2​g​(K)−1>2​g​(L)−1p>2g(K)-1>2g(L)-1, it follows from [20, Theorem 4.4] that

H​F+​(Sp3​(K),g⁡(K))≅H​F+​(S3),H​F+​(Zp​(L),g⁡(K))≅H​F+​(Z).HF^{+}(S^{3}_{p}(K),g(K))\cong HF^{+}(S^{3}),\quad HF^{+}(Z_{p}(L),g(K))\cong HF^{+}(Z).

By (21), we have H​F+​(Z)≅H​F+​(S3)HF^{+}(Z)\cong HF^{+}(S^{3}), hence ZZ is an L-space.

Since p>2​g​(L)−1p>2g(L)-1 and g⁡(K)−1≥g⁡(L)g(K)-1\geq g(L), we have
